About: Relative velocity of a plane

Source

Lecture
Lecture 6 — Galilean relativity and velocity addition.
Simulation
Relative velocity of a plane (collinear, top-down).
Concept
In classical (Galilean) physics, an observer in a frame moving at velocity W relative to the ground measures every object's velocity as v − W.
Serves
Frame-dependence of velocity; the classical addition law u′ = u − V; sets up the SR contrast (light does not obey this).
Inquiry
Alice sees the plane at u = 200 km/h and Bella at V = 100 km/h. What speed does Bella measure for the plane?
Misconception
Students often add Bella's and the plane's speeds (300 km/h) or expect Bella to see the same as Alice (200 km/h). Both are wrong: the answer is u − V = 100 km/h.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Three motions, one road

Let’s meet the cast. Alice stands at the roadside. A train carries Bella East at V = 100 km/h, and a plane flies East overhead at u = 200 km/h — both as Alice measures them.

Here’s the fun part: the very same three motions can be described from the train, or from the cockpit. In every card that follows, we’ll ask what that observer measures.

2 · What Bella measures

Let’s start with Bella. She looks up from the moving train and measures the plane’s velocity. What do you think she gets?

3 · What Bella measures for Alice

Now let’s turn Bella’s attention to the ground. Same train, same plane — but this time Bella measures the velocity of Alice, standing at the roadside. What do you think she gets?

4 · A train faster than the plane

Let’s speed the train up. It’s now doing V = 300 km/h as Alice measures it, with the plane still at u = 200 km/h. What do you think Bella measures for the plane now?

5 · The view from the cockpit

One last switch of viewpoint. The speeds are unchanged: the train at 300 km/h, the plane at 200 km/h, both East for Alice. Now the pilot measures the train. What do you think the pilot gets?

6 · The Galilean velocity transformation

So here’s what ties it all together. Every answer above came from one rule — an observer moving at velocity W relative to the ground measures every velocity as v − W; that’s the Galilean velocity transformation. Relativity replaces it with u′ = (u − V) / (1 − uV/c²): at 200 and 300 km/h the correction uV/c² is about five parts in 10¹⁴, which is why plain subtraction has passed for a law — but set u = c and the formula returns exactly c for every V.

The Physics

Relative velocity of a plane · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A train and a plane both travel East along one road, and three observers measure them: Alice on the ground, Bella on the train, and the pilot. The sim shows how the same motions are described by each observer, and how those descriptions are linked.

What you'll learn

  • How an observer's own motion enters the velocity they read for any object.
  • Which quantities depend on the observer, and which do not.
  • How to find the size and sign of any reading from the ground velocities.
  • Where this everyday rule stops working, and what replaces it.
Speeds as Alice, on the ground, measures them.

What's on screen

  • Alice, Bella and the plane, each with a velocity arrow and a signed km/h label. The arrow's length is proportional to speed, and its direction is the sign.
  • Frame badge (top right): whose frame is active and its speed W relative to the ground. The position ruler is in that frame.
  • Velocities panel: each object's reading in the active frame, with the arithmetic underneath.
See itStart in Alice's ground frame. Watch for: three arrows above the road, and three signed readings in the Velocities panel.

03

Two frames, one clock

A frame is an observer's coordinate system. Bella's frame moves East at V relative to Alice's, with the two origins together at t = 0, and both frames use one shared clock. By time t Bella's origin has moved Vt, so each position she quotes is Alice's minus Vt.

The Galilean transformation. The course notes write the primed frame with a tilde; the sim uses primes.

Because time is shared, a rod has the same length in both frames: mark both ends at one instant and each position loses the same Vt.

The sim's defaults, V = 100 and u = 200 km/h, read in two frames. Each arrow on the right is the left arrow minus W.
Key idea. Galilean relativity assumes time is the same for every observer. The rest of this sheet follows from that one assumption.
See itSwitch to Bella's frame. Watch for: Bella's own reading falling to 0, and the frame badge on the canvas showing W = V.
04

Subtract the frame's speed

Divide the shifted separation by the unshifted time and a velocity rule comes out:

  • Subtract, never add. Both fly East, so Bella is chasing the plane. Adding the speeds would give the closing speed of two objects heading toward each other.
  • Every reading shifts by the same amount. The whole velocity axis slides by W, so the gaps between any two readings stay put.
  • The sign is a direction. If V is larger than u, Bella reads the plane as moving West, although it still flies East for Alice.
The same three velocities read twice: W = 0 above, W = V = 100 below.
See itMake the train faster than the plane (V = 300, u = 200), in Bella's frame. Watch for: the plane's arrow pointing West, with a negative reading.
05

Any observer, the same rule

W is the active frame's ground velocity: 0 for Alice, V for Bella, u for the pilot. Every reading in the Velocities panel is the ground velocity minus W. The pilot's frame works exactly like Bella's.

V u

These sliders move the sim too.

See itSwitch to the pilot's frame. Watch for: the plane's own reading falling to 0, and the frame badge on the canvas showing W = u.
06

What every observer agrees on

  • Differences. Subtract any two readings in one frame and the shift W cancels. The plane's velocity relative to the train is u − V in all three frames.
  • Accelerations. V is constant, so differentiating again gives a′ = a. Mass and force are the same in both frames too, so F = ma keeps its form in every frame that moves at constant velocity.
  • No special frame. Among frames moving at constant velocity, the ground is one choice, not the true one. No mechanical experiment inside a train at constant velocity can tell that it moves.
See itVisit all three frames in turn and compare the plane with the train in each. Watch for: the same difference every time, though every reading changes.
07

Where plain subtraction fails

The sim always subtracts exactly. The relativistic law, shown here for comparison, divides the same difference by a factor that includes c = 299 792 458 m/s ≈ 1.08 × 10⁹ km/h:

  • At road speeds the factor equals 1 to within 10⁻¹². Even at V = 400 and u = 600 km/h, uV/c² is about 2 × 10⁻¹³, so no road experiment can tell the two laws apart.
  • For light the laws disagree. Subtraction predicts c − V. Put u = c in the relativistic law and every observer reads c, whatever V is.
The plane arrows are to scale. The dashed c − V is schematic: at V = 100 km/h the real shortfall would be about 1 part in 10⁷.
See itSet the fastest settings (V = 400, u = 600) in Bella's frame. Watch for: the plane read as exactly 600 − 400 = +200 km/h, with uV/c² of about 2 × 10⁻¹³.
08

Where it matters

  • Navigation. An aircraft's velocity over the ground is its velocity through the air plus the air's velocity over the ground. This is the same bookkeeping, and it is how groundspeed is found from airspeed and wind.
  • Overtaking. A car at 90 km/h passing a lorry at 80 km/h closes at 10 km/h. The time to pass depends on that relative speed, not on 90.
  • Galileo's ship. Galileo argued that nothing seen or done below deck on a smoothly moving ship reveals its motion. Section 06 gives the modern reason: accelerations are the same in every constant-velocity frame.
Go deeper: when the correction matters
  • The factor 1 − uV/c² matters only when u and V are a sizeable fraction of c. With u = 0.9c and V = 0.5c, subtraction gives 0.4c, but the relativistic law gives 0.4c / 0.55 ≈ 0.727c.
  • For |u| and |V| below c, the relativistic result never reaches c. Lecture 7 shows what replaces absolute time.
09

Summary

In one line. An observer moving at W reads every ground velocity v as v − W. That rule is exact if time is absolute, and at road speeds it matches relativity to better than 1 part in 10¹².

Key points

  • A velocity belongs to an object and an observer together. Change the observer and the reading changes.
  • Readings shift by W; differences between readings, and accelerations, do not.
  • The sign of a reading is a direction in the active frame, East positive.
  • For light the rule fails: the relativistic law gives c in every frame.

Common mix-ups

  • "Bella reads the plane at 300 km/h." Adding gives the closing speed of objects heading toward each other. Both fly East, so she reads u − V.
  • "Alice is at rest, so Bella reads 0 for her." Alice is at rest only in her own frame. In Bella's frame the roadside moves West at V.
  • "A negative reading means the plane turned around." The sign is a direction in the active frame. At V = 300 the plane still flies East for Alice.

Things to try on your own

  • Set V = 250 and u = 200. Work out all nine readings (three objects, three frames), then check each one in the Velocities panel.
  • Find a setting where the pilot reads Bella at exactly 0, then read the plane in Bella's frame.
